messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Lucian Bauer is a 49-year-old European-born fashion designer living in New York with his wife of twenty-two years. He was referred for psychological assessment following a visit to his primary care physician, who noted significant weight loss, disrupted sleep, and what Lucian described, with characteristic understatement, as "a problem concentrating on my work." His PCL-5 score of 77 places him in the severe range of post-traumatic stress, and across the intake sessions a coherent and devastating picture emerged.

Approximately eight months ago, Lucian's adult son, Matteo, was involved in a serious road accident while Lucian was driving. The collision occurred on a rain-slicked highway outside the city on a Sunday evening. Lucian remembers the moment of impact with a kind of terrible precision — the sound of shattering glass, the way Matteo's head snapped sideways, the specific orange glow of the emergency lights that arrived later — but the minutes immediately following are almost entirely gone. He knows he must have called for help. He knows he spoke to paramedics. But those minutes exist as a blank, and it is the blankness itself that torments him, because what he has come to believe, with a conviction that no reassurance has been able to touch, is that he failed to act quickly enough. The partial clarity of the memory — some moments crystalline, others completely absent — has become evidence, in his mind, of a moral failure so severe it cannot be looked at directly. When the memory surfaces, as it does involuntarily and without warning, the guilt is immediate and overwhelming, and on more than one occasion he has had to leave a client meeting abruptly because he could no longer function.

It is this quality of the memory — its power to flood him entirely — that has driven Lucian toward a set of strategies that now structure his entire day. He keeps his mind occupied at all times, filling every available moment with work, music, podcasts, conversation, anything that prevents the stillness in which the memory tends to arrive. He tries, with considerable effort, to suppress any thought that edges toward the accident, and he has stopped making plans for the future — not consciously at first, but gradually, as though some part of him decided that anticipating anything was too dangerous. His studio, once a place of expansive creative thinking driven by seasonal collections and long-range vision, has become a place of pure present-tense execution. Colleagues have noticed. A junior designer recently asked whether Lucian was planning to show at the spring event, and his inability to answer — not evasion, but genuine incapacity — marked a professional turning point that his wife has since described as alarming.

The threat Lucian lives under is not abstract. He experiences strong physical reactions when something reminds him of that evening — the sound of rain on a window, the particular quality of highway noise, even the orange of a warning light on a dashboard — and these reactions arrive before any conscious thought, as a surge of physical alarm that leaves him shaking. He carries a persistent sense of horror and guilt that colours his emotional life entirely, and his nights are rarely restful, his sleep broken by a vigilance he cannot switch off. This state of chronic threat feeds directly back into the memory: when he is physiologically aroused, the fragments of that evening become more intrusive, more insistent, pressing through whatever distraction he has constructed. The strategies that were meant to contain the memory instead seem to sharpen it — suppression, he has found, does not make the images smaller but makes their return more forceful, and the very act of keeping himself perpetually occupied has begun to feel less like coping and more like proof that he cannot survive contact with what happened.

Lucian sought help, finally, after Matteo — who has largely recovered physically — told him gently that he felt his father had become unreachable. What Lucian is most afraid of is that the guilt he carries is not a symptom but a verdict. What he is most hoping for, though he struggles to say it plainly, is that someone might help him find out what happened in those missing minutes — and perhaps, in finding it, release him from the weight of not knowing.
